documents.abstract: Railway signaling software must satisfy strict requirements—clarity, completeness, verifiability, and traceability—from the specification phase. KRS-SG-0069 requirements are written in Korean natural language, making manual structuring costly and expert-dependent. I propose a semi-automated framework combining LLM-based structuring with deterministic verification. Analysis of 94 requirements identified seven defect types mapped to EN 50128 clause 7.2.4 violations. The framework comprises four modules: M1 classifies requirements; M2 converts them into a six-element boilerplate via Chain-of-Thought prompting; M3 validates drafts through a four-layer rule engine; M4 generates state transition models, test cases, and a traceability matrix. The LLM is confined to draft generation, while safety judgments are delegated to deterministic engines and formal validators. This paper presents an architectural foundation; quantitative evaluation and broader applicability remain as future work.

The article examines the mechanisms of public administration for ensuring the quality of higher education in Ukraine through the prism of the classifications established in the scholarly discourse, as well as through the practices of their functioning and their actual impact on the international competitiveness of domestic higher education institutions. The methodological basis of the research combines the analysis of regulatory and legal acts, programme documents of the international and national levels, statistical data of the National Agency for Higher Education Quality Assurance, and a comparative analysis of the dynamics of the positioning of Ukrainian universities in the leading international rankings during 2022–2026. A contradiction has been identified between the architectonics of building the higher education quality assurance system and the comparatively low positioning of Ukrainian universities in international rankings (Quacquarelli Symonds World University Rankings; Times Higher Education World University Rankings; Academic Ranking of World Universities, ShanghaiRanking). In particular, it has been established that the number of Ukrainian universities represented in the QS World University Rankings decreased from 11 in 2023 to 4 in 2026, while the highest position of domestic institutions in the Times Higher Education ranking has consistently remained within the 801–1000 group despite the quantitative growth of their representation. The exhaustion of the potential of the traditional regulatory-legal, organisational- administrative and economic mechanisms of public administration in the higher education sphere has been substantiated, along with the need to search for new mechanisms of public administration for ensuring quality. The article also offers proposals on the necessity of applying innovative mechanisms for ensuring the quality of higher education, namely those grounded in the toolkit of artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and robotic process automation, the practical significance of which is confirmed by international experience and the analytical priorities of the national quality assurance system.
topics: Education and Social Development in Ukraine

documents.abstract: Higher education plays a pivotal role in shaping a nation's economic growth, technological advancement, and social development. India possesses one of the world's largest higher education systems, comprising over one thousand universities and thousands of colleges that collectively educate millions of students annually. Despite significant expansion in institutional capacity and enrolment over the past two decades, maintaining quality remains a major concern. Challenges such as inadequate infrastructure, faculty shortages, disparities in access, limited research productivity, employability gaps, insufficient industry-academia collaboration, governance issues, and unequal digital access continue to impede the realization of globally competitive higher education. Simultaneously, transformative initiatives including the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, digital learning platforms, research funding reforms, international collaborations, multidisciplinary education, and the integration of artificial intelligence present unprecedented opportunities for systemic improvement. This review critically examines the current status of higher education quality in India by synthesizing evidence from government reports, policy documents, and contemporary scholarly literature. The paper discusses the multidimensional challenges affecting educational quality and evaluates emerging opportunities driven by technological innovation, quality assurance mechanisms, competency-based curricula, and global academic partnerships. Furthermore, it proposes strategic recommendations to strengthen governance, faculty development, research ecosystems, institutional autonomy, accreditation, digital transformation, and employability. The study concludes that achieving sustainable excellence in higher education requires coordinated efforts among policymakers, regulatory agencies, academic institutions, industry, and society. A learner-centric, technology-enabled, research-oriented, and globally connected higher education system will be fundamental to realizing India's vision of becoming a global knowledge economy by 2047.

ABSTRACT Electrochemical advanced oxidation processes (EAOPs) have become a prominent tool in wastewater remediation of refractory organic pollutants due to their versatility and ability to generate powerful, in situ oxidant species—predominantly hydroxyl radicals (•OH). Concurrently, quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models have emerged as vital tools for predicting activity in high‐priority areas like drug development and toxicity. In this review, we address the application of QSARs in decoding reactivity within electrooxidation processes. We trace their evolution from early origins using the Hammett parameter () as a molecular descriptor to quantum chemical descriptors—such as , ionization potentials (IPs), and Fukui functions—and finally to advanced machine learning (ML) approaches like graph neural networks (GNNs) designed to navigate complex real wastewater matrices. Additionally, we highlight the anode as a core mechanistic variable that dictates oxidant selectivity. Finally, we discuss the primary limitations hindering ML adoption in EAOPs—including small training sets, a lack of electrochemical‐specific datasets, limited water‐matrix transferability, black‐box interpretability, and conflicting optimization metrics—and explore emerging strategies to overcome them, such as transfer learning, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and physics‐informed ML.

This volume examines one of the most important teacher–scholar projects of our time: innovating pedagogies and ethics in the age of artificial intelligence (AI). The volume brings together scholarship in three sections: Introductions, Digital Agency and Giving Students Voice, and Embodied Pedagogies. In this volume, we curate scholarship that engages with pedagogical governance for educators, digital storytelling, inclusive pedagogy, discussion boards, online student engagement, autoethnography, documentary-making, ecological consciousness, study practices, community-centered learning, and Geographic Information System (GIS) mapping. Taken together, this body of research demonstrates that meaningful learning is not only cognitive but also emotional, relational, and contextual, which requires pedagogies that attend to empathy, belonging, and lived experience. Across diverse contexts, educators are provided with pedagogical tools to support students in developing critical thinking and reflection skills while also fostering social responsibility and a commitment to the common good. All these elements are essential to this timely, interdisciplinary teacher–scholar project to support ethical AI in education.

Analytical chemistry plays an essential role in the identification, separation, quantification, and characterization of pharmaceutical substances. Recent technological developments have introduced advanced analytical approaches with improved sensitivity, accuracy, selectivity, speed, and reliability.[1] This review focuses on recent research in chromatography, mass spectrometry, spectroscopy, biosensors, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML), and Green Analytical Chemistry. Modern chromatographic and mass spectrometric techniques enable efficient separation, structural characterization, impurity profiling, and sensitive analysis of complex samples. Spectroscopic techniques provide rapid and non-destructive characterization, while biosensors offer sensitive, rapid, and potentially portable detection systems. AI/ML approaches are increasingly applied for analytical data processing, prediction, pattern recognition, and method optimization. Green analytical approaches aim to minimize hazardous solvents, waste generation, energy consumption, and sample requirements while maintaining analytical performance.[2] The review compares the methodologies, major findings, strengths, limitations, and research gaps reported in recent studies. Overall, the integration of advanced instrumentation, intelligent data analysis, biosensing technologies, and sustainable analytical practices is expected to contribute to the development of faster, more sensitive, reliable, automated, and environmentally sustainable pharmaceutical analytical methods.

Caries risk assessment (CRA) is intended to estimate an individual's likelihood of developing new caries lesions or experiencing lesion progression over a defined period so that preventive, diagnostic and recall strategies can be tailored. Contemporary CRA is changing rapidly. Established approaches such as Cariogram, Caries Management by Risk Assessment (CAMBRA), professional checklists and risk-based care pathways are increasingly being supplemented by statistical prediction models, machine learning, digital self-assessment, salivary and microbiome biomarkers, and population-specific tools. This critical narrative review evaluates whether these developments have improved prognosis rather than merely increased technical complexity. Literature published principally from 2015 to 8 August 2026 was examined, while earlier seminal studies were retained when necessary to establish concepts and validation history. The synthesis distinguishes future-event prediction from cross-sectional detection or classification, because this distinction is frequently blurred in the recent literature. The strongest and most reproducible conventional predictor remains previous or current caries experience, while social conditions, fluoride exposure, plaque, diet, salivary function and life-course factors modify risk. Established multifactorial tools can structure clinical reasoning and risk-linked care, but external validation remains uneven and evidence that their use itself improves patient outcomes is limited. Machine-learning studies often report promising discrimination, yet many rely on cross-sectional outcomes, internal validation, small samples or incomplete calibration and clinical-utility assessment. Prospective cohorts demonstrate that simple, readily collected predictors can perform competitively, challenging assumptions that algorithmic complexity necessarily improves care. Salivary, microbiome and genetic approaches remain biologically informative but are not yet sufficiently standardised or externally validated for routine prognostic use. The most important recent trend is therefore methodological rather than technological: CRA is moving towards explicit prediction horizons, transparent validation, calibration, decision-linked utility, population transportability and repeated reassessment. Future progress will depend on prospective multicentre validation and impact studies that compare complex models against parsimonious clinical baselines and test whether risk-guided decisions improve outcomes without widening inequalities.

Generative AI is reshaping video production from a set of isolated tools into a core production infrastructure. This chapter presents an integrative value-chain framework showing how AI transforms pre-production, production, post-production, and distribution. It identifies four major shifts: workflow compression, creative augmentation, scale and personalization, and disintermediation. The chapter also examines the tension between democratization, in which low-cost AI tools empower small studios, educators, and creators in emerging economies, and consolidation, in which powerful firms control foundation models, compute, data, and distribution. Using cases on virtual production, AI-assisted localization, and the 2023 Hollywood labor agreements, it discusses key governance issues, including labor displacement, intellectual property disputes, content authenticity, and audience trust. It argues that AI is reorganizing video production as an economic system and offers recommendations for scholars, practitioners, and policymakers, especially in the Global South.

ABSTRACT This reflective article identifies three interconnected themes for advancing scholarship on new technology, work and employment. First, it calls for stronger theorisation of technology and deeper engagement with the political economy of Big Tech and AI. Attending to the material and political dimensions of technological systems is vital for challenging dominant narratives that present technologically driven change as inevitable. Second, the article argues for widening the empirical scope of research beyond the “new, new technologies,” while overlooking less visible sectors and the differing experiences of adopters and non‐adopters within the same industries. Broadening the empirical field and methodological repertoire would illuminate the uneven and variegated nature of digitalisation. Third, the article emphasises the importance of historical contextualisation. Situating contemporary developments within longer trajectories of workplace transformation is essential for understanding ongoing challenges and informing research on work futures.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organisational decision-making, creating opportunities for innovation and sustainability while intensifying concerns about accountability, transparency, stakeholder responsibility and human oversight. This structured theory-building integrative review synthesises a purposively bounded corpus of 35 unique works on responsible AI, AI governance, responsible leadership and organisational sustainability. Responsible AI Governance (RAIG) is conceptualised as a multidimensional organisational capability: the repeatable, coordinated and adaptive capacity through which responsible AI principles are translated into governance structures, decision processes, accountability arrangements, stakeholder relationships, human oversight and assurance across the AI lifecycle. Six interdependent dimensions are specified: ethical-strategic alignment, accountability architecture, human oversight and agency, stakeholder inclusion, transparency and assurance and lifecycle governance and adaptability. Responsible leadership is positioned as an antecedent managerial microfoundation rather than a constitutive dimension of RAIG. The framework separates sustainability from the content of RAIG and theorises sustainable organisational and stakeholder outcomes as consequences of effective governance. Propositions and a staged research programme establish a foundation for construct operationalisation, cross-context validation and subsequent nomological testing.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence now shapes digital marketing, influencing targeting, personalization, pricing, content creation, and customer engagement. However, its use creates risks including algorithmic bias, personalization–privacy tensions, manipulative interface design, and declining consumer trust following AI disclosure. This chapter addresses a gap by integrating these risks with the design and governance mechanisms needed for responsible AI in digital marketing. Drawing on research in marketing, information systems, public administration, and law, it examines algorithmic risk, consumer trust, explainability, transparency, governance, and regulation. The review identifies consumer trust as the key mechanism linking algorithmic risk to marketing outcomes and proposes an integrated framework in which fairness auditing, consent-based data practices, responsible interface design, and explainability act as design levers, while governance and regulation establish implementation conditions. The chapter argues that responsible AI can help manage algorithmic risk and build trust.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming digital marketing by enabling automation and personalization. For micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), AI offers opportunities to enhance competitiveness despite limited resources. However, adoption introduces risks such as privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, and cybersecurity threats that may undermine customer trust. These challenges are especially critical in emerging economies facing financial and technical constraints. The primary objective of this chapter is to systematically investigate the intersection of AI and digital marketing strategies among MSMEs in Oman, aligning responsible practices with Oman Vision 2040. Employing a qualitative, conceptual desk research methodology built on a systematic literature review, this study applies Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE), Trust, and Stakeholder frameworks to identify operational barriers and propose a sustainable growth framework centered on transparency, fairness, accountability, privacy, and human oversight.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: As generative AI tools rapidly integrate into higher education—assisting with instruction, content generation, student evaluation, and research—universities face a complex landscape of ethical challenges. Drawing on a detailed review of current scholarship, this study evaluates the integration of generative AI, focusing on ongoing debates surrounding academic integrity, authorship, and the reliability of machine-generated output. Beyond individual misconduct, it addresses broader systemic risks, including algorithmic bias, data privacy vulnerabilities, detector inaccuracies, and the urgent need for clear institutional governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are rapidly reshaping university learning environments, yet pedagogical and ethical frameworks have not developed at the same pace as their adoption. Adopting a multidisciplinary approach, this study combines empirical evidence from a survey of 117 undergraduate Engineering and Health Sciences students with the pedagogical perspectives of university lecturers. It examines how students currently use GenAI and how these tools can be meaningfully integrated into teaching and learning. Findings show that students’ first exposure to GenAI is mainly driven by informal social media channels rather than institutional guidance, resulting in uneven and often unguided adoption. The study also identifies a “contradictory profile” in 11% of the sample: students who perceive GenAI use as a form of cheating while also expressing a strong demand for formal training on its academic integration. From the lecturers’ perspective, GenAI offers opportunities to support content creation, assessment design, and instructional workflows, provided that human-led teaching remains central. By integrating observed student behaviors with expert recommendations, this research proposes an ethical framework and practical guidelines for the responsible integration of GenAI in higher education. The study highlights the urgent need for institutional policies that address emerging socio-ethical tensions and ensure that GenAI enhances, rather than circumvents, foundational knowledge, academic integrity, and critical thinking.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The Revolutionizing Tertiary Education for Africa's Thriving AI Economy and Workforce (RetAIn) project presents a comprehensive, multi-method investigation into the conditions, constraints, and catalysts shaping Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption across African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). Deploying both qualitative multi-stakeholders Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) from three African countries (Ghana, Rwanda, Namibia) and a quantitative cross-country survey across five Sub-Saharan African nations (Ghana, Rwanda, Namibia, Kenya, and Zambia), this study produces a richly triangulated account of AI integration dynamics on the continent. The FGD strand revealed a stark divergence in national AI trajectories: Rwanda operates under a strong top-down policy vision hindered by institutional rigidity; Namibia exhibits pragmatic institutional adaptability constrained by geographic and economic smallness; and Ghana demonstrates emergent, bottom-up innovation within a national policy vacuum. The survey strand, drawing on 156 responses across five countries, corroborated these qualitative tensions, documenting widespread recognition of AI's strategic importance alongside limited structured engagement, persistent infrastructure deficits, and marked equity barriers, particularly for women, vulnerable groups, rural students, and part-time workers. From both methods, a unifying finding emerges: AI integration in African HEIs consistently fails when technical adoption outpaces social, pedagogical, and governance co-evolution. The study argues for context-specific, socio-technically grounded strategies that pair curriculum co-design with robust industry partnerships, that centre equity and cultural relevance, and build governance frameworks capable of guiding, rather than chasing, technological change.

Modern translator training faces a structural mismatch: technology is typically taught as a set of isolated modules, one tool per topic, while professional translation practice treats these same tools as an interconnected workflow in which a single instrument routinely performs functions attributed to several distinct stages. This article reframes the transla- tion process as a technological chain comprising four interrelated components – pre-translation analysis, CAT-assisted translation supported by an AI agent, quality management, and file preparation – and argues that these components are better represented as a network of overlapping actions than as a linear sequence of self-contained stages. Drawing on both theoretical models of translator competence (PACTE’s instrumental competence, the EMT framework) and empirical studies of specific tools and stages, the article identifies a gap between well-established theoretical support for cross- cutting technical competence and its still-fragmented empirical and classroom validation. The study demonstrates, through classroom examples – including the pre-editing of auto-generated video subtitles using regular expressions and a compar- ative analysis of PDF-document translation across several CAT environments – that a single technological action routinely crosses the boundaries between the four proposed stages, undermining the pedagogical logic of modular instruction. The article proposes a network model of the translation technological chain, in which the four components function as condi- tional nodes connected by feedback and cross-cutting links rather than fixed sequential order, and grounds this model in the broader concept of a translator’s digital literacy. The findings support a concrete pedagogical principle: technical com- petence formation should be organized around cross-cutting, project-based assignments that require students to move across several nodes of the model, rather than around isolated tool-specific modules. The article concludes by identifying directions for further research, including the applicability of the proposed model to team-based translation workflows and an unresolved gap between the documented professional importance of quality-management tools and students’ compar- atively modest perception of their value.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter aims to explore the intricate relationship between authenticity, trust, and consumer loyalty in influencer marketing. Authenticity is pivotal in influencer marketing, where consumers, inundated with curated content, crave honesty and relatable experiences. Genuine passion from influencers for brands builds trust and transparency, connecting brands with consumers. This connection fosters positive brand perceptions and purchase intent.. By demystifying the role of authenticity in influencer marketing, this chapter aims to empower brands to circumnavigate the digital landscape effectively and build genuine relationships with their target audiences. Ultimately, it pursues to underwrite to a more transparent and trustworthy influencer marketing environment that benefits both consumers and brands. However, the advent of AI Technology and the rapid progress in this field have helped marketers to identify these challenges and solve their inherent problems. Also, AI today truly provides new and exciting avenues for marketing companies.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Digital transformation and artificial intelligence are redefining how people access and navigate community healthcare. Concurrently, community nursing services are facing a sustained workforce decline. While digital nurse leadership has matured in many acute organisations, community nurses are increasingly expected to deliver technology-enabled care without equivalent leadership structures, support or career pathways. In this article, the author details a proposal for a digital specialist community public health nurse (digital SCPHN) role framework. The author describes the digital SCPHN as first and foremost a clinician, with digital capability as an essential enhancement rather than a replacement of core nursing objectives. Positioned as a digital translator and champion within community teams, the digital SCPHN helps people to navigate complex digital healthcare systems while supporting their colleagues through technology-enabled care prioritisation, secure safeguarding communication and community risk insight. The author also outlines six actionable recommendations for front-line nurses, team leads and system commissioners to strengthen community nursing impact, improve digital literacy and ensure equitable, person-centred care in digitally enabled neighbourhood healthcare systems.

Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct Sci$Π$vot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models and reasoning effort settings is 63.5%, compared with 73.4% for fresh researchers. At medium effort, every model achieves lower accuracy with the project record than without it, and reconsideration does not consistently improve overall accuracy. Even with a human-corrected alternative available, frontier models struggle with the selected research decisions, while Sci$Π$vot supports systematic evaluation of scientific judgment for LLM agents.

This working paper constitutes the first deliverable under the EFSA contract RTD/2023/OP/0011 – Lot 1 on Foresight on Demand in Science, Technology, Research and Innovation Policy, implemented within the framework of multi-agency foresight on One Health and authorised by the European Commission, DG Research & Innovation, G1 – Common R&I Strategy and Foresight Service. It examines the relevance of the One Health approach for a broad range of European institutions and agencies and argues that One Health has become an increasingly important framework for addressing the complex and interdependent challenges facing the European Union. These challenges include emerging infectious diseases, antimicrobial and antifungal resistance, environmental pollution, climate change, food insecurity, mental health pressures, and widening social inequalities, all of which cut across traditional sectoral and institutional boundaries. The report situates One Health within its broader conceptual and policy context. It shows that the approach has evolved from earlier biomedical understandings centred on zoonotic disease and veterinary-public health cooperation into a wider framework linking human, animal, plant, and environmental health. In line with the recommendations of the European Commission’s Group of Chief Scientific Advisors, the report adopts the OHHLEP definition of One Health as an integrated and unifying approach aimed at balancing and optimizing the health of humans, animals, plants, and ecosystems. At the same time, it underlines that important ambiguities remain concerning the interpretation, scope, and operationalisation of the concept, especially in the context of European governance. The report therefore not only maps One Health as a thematic field but also examines how it can serve as a practical basis for stronger coordination among EU agencies and institutions. A central finding is that One Health is already relevant to a wide constellation of EU bodies, even if this relevance is not always explicitly recognised or institutionally coordinated. The report highlights the roles of DG SANTE, DG ENV, DG CLIMA, DG AGRI, and the Joint Research Centre, as well as agencies such as EFSA, EMA, ECDC, EEA, ECHA, EUDA, EU-OSHA, Frontex, EIGE, and ETF. These actors contribute complementary expertise across food safety, infectious disease monitoring, environmental protection, chemical safety, medicines regulation, occupational health, social inequalities, and preparedness. The report notes that cooperation has already advanced through initiatives such as the ONE Conference, the cross-agency One Health task force, and joint work on zoonoses and antimicrobial resistance. However, it also finds that collaboration remains uneven, fragmented, and often dependent on issue-specific rather than strategic coordination. Existing efforts show strong potential, but the absence of a fully integrated governance architecture continues to limit the EU’s capacity to translate One Health into a genuinely shared and anticipatory policy framework. On this basis, the report develops a broad and integrated overview of the main scientific themes currently shaping the One Health agenda. These include infectious diseases and health security, veterinary medical products, antimicrobial and antifungal resistance, environmental and climate-related health risks, animal health and welfare, public health and disease prevention, sustainable food systems, inequalities and governance, digitalisation and health, and education and training. A major contribution of the report is that it expands the One Health agenda beyond its more established focus on zoonoses and AMR. It argues that issues such as chemical pollution, microplastics, PFAS, unsafe food systems, occupational health, illicit drugs, mental health, militarization, nuclear risks, and the health implications of geopolitical change must also be considered within a One Health framework because they arise from and reinforce the interdependence of environmental, animal, and human health. The report therefore presents One Health not as a narrow technical field, but as a broader framework for understanding and governing systemic and interacting risks. The report also emphasizes that the One Health perspective is closely aligned with broader EU strategic priorities. It shows that One Health contributes not only to public health protection, but also to goals related to sustainable prosperity, food security, preparedness, climate resilience, social fairness, and democratic legitimacy. In this sense, One Health is framed as a governance approach capable of linking prevention, resilience, and sustainability across domains that are too often treated separately. The report repeatedly stresses that challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, environmental degradation, food insecurity, and health inequalities cannot be addressed adequately through isolated policy responses. Rather, they require integrated surveillance, coordinated foresight, and stronger institutional mechanisms capable of connecting evidence, preparedness, and action across sectors and scales. A further important conclusion is that One Health must be treated as both a scientific and institutional innovation agenda. The report identifies the need for stronger inter- and transdisciplinary collaboration, improved data sharing, harmonised surveillance systems, and clearer coordination mechanisms at EU level. It supports the view that the European Union should adopt a more coherent One Health strategy, backed by adequate resources, shared infrastructures, and long-term political support. Education and training are also identified as crucial pillars. One Health concepts should be integrated into academic, professional, and public learning environments, while digital tools, artificial intelligence, and data systems should be developed in line with ethical, inclusive, and sustainable principles. At the same time, the report warns that digitalisation, if poorly governed, may reproduce inequalities, deepen data divides, and generate new environmental burdens. In its final section, the report moves from thematic mapping to strategic foresight. It identifies a series of emerging and cross-cutting areas that merit particular attention in future collaboration. These include cross-border health threats and joint preparedness, chemicals and environmental exposures, illicit drugs and their environmental and social dimensions, climate change and health inequalities, social determinants of health, mental health, digitalisation, and militarization. Across all these areas, the report underscores the need for strengthened multi-agency collaboration and more systematic data sharing. It argues that the EU already possesses many of the institutional building blocks required for a stronger One Health approach, but that these assets need to be connected more effectively through coordinated foresight, shared analytical tools, and common strategic priorities. Overall, the report presents One Health as a necessary and forward-looking framework for European governance. It shows that the health of people, animals, plants, and ecosystems is increasingly shaped by interconnected pressures that no single institution, sector, or Member State can manage alone. By embedding One Health more firmly in research agendas, legislative initiatives, surveillance systems, education, and inter-agency cooperation, the European Union can improve its capacity to anticipate and respond to multidimensional threats while also advancing sustainability, equity, and resilience. In this sense, One Health is not merely a conceptual lens, but a practical foundation for future European collaboration in science, regulation, and strategic policy development.

documents.abstract: With the advent of Internet of Things technologies and intelligent edge computing systems, the surface of cyber-attacks has been increasingly growing, which results in the problem of network security in distributed systems. This chapter will provide a review of intelligent intrusion detection methods using AI for secure intelligent edge ecosystems in the IoT. The chapter will discuss how machine learning, deep learning, and federated learning models are used together with edge computing systems to increase detection accuracy, reduce the time needed for detection, and maintain scalability while preserving data privacy. Furthermore, the proposed framework takes into account explainable artificial intelligence, privacy-preserving learning, and deployment techniques to overcome problems related to limited resource constraints of edge devices. Also, this chapter explores present security issues, application scenarios, implementation issues, and future perspectives, such as zero trust architecture, collaborative edge intelligence, and autonomous cyber defense systems.

Abstract Query optimization is a crucial problem in database systems that has been studied for decades. Learned query optimizers (LQOs) can improve performance over time by incorporating feedback; however, they suffer from cold-start issues and often require retraining when workloads shift or schemas change. We initially proposed SEFRQO, a Self-Evolving Fine-tuned RAG-based Query Optimizer, which leverages fine-tuned LLMs to address these challenges and uses in-context learning to achieve continuous evolution. However, its system design relies on the assumption of repetitive query workloads, requires executing queries statically upon their first encounter (incurring extra overhead), and utilizes only partial feedback from the best historical records (insufficient feedback design). In this paper, we present SEFRQO-Plus, which resolves the above limitations. First, we design a feedback-oriented vector database with query structure-aware embeddings to support effective similarity search, and we incorporate multi-layered histories as references to enrich the feedback. Then, we enhance the prompt optimization workflow by utilizing multi-dimensional historical feedback to drive continuous self-evolution. Moreover, we provide formal theoretical proofs to validate the advantages of our customized query group relative policy optimization. Evaluations show that SEFRQO-Plus outperforms state-of-the-art LQOs, achieving reductions of 66.52% and 69.79% in query latency for the complete CEB and Stack workloads, respectively, compared to PostgreSQL. SEFRQO-Plus achieves an additional 15% improvement over the initial SEFRQO. Moreover, it generalizes effectively across multiple workloads and scenarios, and even across different DBMSes.

Abstract Background In recent years, the availability of digital therapeutic apps in medicine, digital therapeutics (DTx), has significantly increased. To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of DTx, an increasing number of scientific studies have been conducted in this field. Several authors have pointed out that a standardized approach to DTx evaluation is relevant to improving the comparability of apps in the future. Currently, it is unclear how study authors proceed when selecting outcomes and measurement methods (O&M) for DTx studies. Objective The primary aim of this study was to investigate how study authors currently select O&M in DTx studies, specifically for applications delivered in the form of apps. The secondary objectives were to collect suggestions for improving the comparability of DTx apps and studies in the future and to examine whether core outcome sets (COS) could represent a possible solution for enhancing comparability. Methods This study was based on 19 semistructured interviews. All interview partners had prior experience in planning and conducting DTx studies. The interviews were conducted between August 2024 and November 2024. Subsequently, qualitative data analysis was performed according to Kuckartz and Rädiker using a deductive-inductive research approach. Results The results of this study showed that the methodological approach for selecting O&M in DTx studies was primarily based on research, as well as on personal prior experience and individual ideas. Interview participants indicated that when selecting O&M, they particularly focused on aspects such as scientific quality criteria or practical implementation and feasibility. A suggestion for achieving better comparability of DTx studies in the future was to use standardized O&M per therapeutic indication area. Almost all interviewees considered COS to be a suitable approach for improving the comparability of DTx and associated studies. However, we also identified critical perspectives that questioned their application. Conclusions Across professional groups, both commonalities and differences were observed in methodological approaches as well as in the selection of O&M in DTx studies. To improve the comparability of DTx interventions and trials, several approaches have been developed, for example, through the use of guidance frameworks, artificial intelligence programs, or the establishment of COS. However, further research is warranted to advance this field.

The emergence of the artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) has led to increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks. For many of these threats, labeled training data are scarce or unavailable, which increases the need for label-free intrusion detection systems. To address this issue, this study proposes a self-supervised one-class TabNet framework, termed SS-OC-TabNet, for intrusion detection in tabular network traffic. The framework combines self-supervised representation learning and one-class compactness learning within a two-stage training process. In the first stage, masked-feature reconstruction is used to learn the feature structure of normal traffic from unlabeled data. In the second stage, a hypersphere compactness objective is applied to make the latent representations of normal traffic more compact for anomaly detection. TabNet is used as the backbone to support sequential feature selection, which also improves interpretability. The proposed model was evaluated on the NSL-KDD dataset and further validated through comparison with related works on the ToN-IoT dataset, achieving an accuracy of 93.20% with a false alarm rate of 2.13%. Further, the interpretability results show which traffic features influence the model's decisions. The compact design and low computational complexity of the proposed framework also support energy-efficient deployment in resource-constrained AIoT environments. These results indicate that SS-OC-TabNet is a viable tool for label-free intrusion detection in AIoT environments. documents.abstract: Studies suggest that computer workers may benefit from cycling workstations; however, little is known about the sex-specific mechanistic impacts of cycling on computer work-related risk factors. Twenty-six computer users (14 females) underwent two 60-min sessions of typing: one sitting, and one lightly cycling, while performance, symptoms and electromyography were recorded. Results show that males' typing speed was lower during cycling than sitting, while females' performance remained similar between conditions (Sex × Condition, p = 0.029). Neck/shoulder and visual discomfort were lower during cycling for both sexes, with females experiencing less neck/shoulder discomfort than males (Sex × Condition × Time, p = 0.006). Neck/shoulder muscle activation increased with time during sitting but decreased during cycling, especially in females. Low back muscle activity was higher during cycling, particularly in females (Sex × Condition × Time interaction, p = 0.046). Findings suggest sex-specific responses to cycling during computer work.

This study examines collaborative learning design with a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) co-pilot among in-service university English teachers in China. In a between-subjects experiment ( N = 60), epistemic network analysis (ENA) was used to model the situated discourse structures of team dialogues, complemented by thematic analysis of interviews. AI-supported teams achieved higher overall scores on a rubric covering constructive alignment, Universal Design for Learning principles, and other aspects of learning design. ENA identified task-specific differences in collaborative discourse, with AI-supported teams displaying a more interconnected and learner-centered network. Participants described the AI as a pedagogical conscience and an intellectual sparring partner whose prompts kept professional judgment visible during the design process. The findings suggest that, in complex professional tasks, GenAI may support reflection and pedagogical reasoning alongside design work.

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents translate software interfaces at scale, yet production evidence on what breaks—and which safeguards catch it—is nearly absent: a 2026 mapping study of localization testing retained 24 primary studies, though none on LLM-driven localization. We report a multi-case study of fourteen shipped mobile apps by one developer (ten iOS, four Android; 40–76 locales; roughly 347,000 units) at five maturity levels. Mining the repositories (catalogs, 4473 commits, process documents, tooling), we code defects into thirteen classes in two waves, the second under a frozen codebook, and map each to its detecting layer. Translation quality is not independently measured; the defect record is a lower bound. Of 468 commit-anchored defects, process and coverage gaps—strings escaping the pipeline—are modal in each wave (26.7% and 27.5%); placeholder errors are near-absent (9 in 347,000 units). LLM judges are the largest operational detector (26.7%), ahead of humans (16.0%) and validators (13.7%), yet 127 defects (27.1%) escaped every layer until our audit. What escapes tracks validator scope, not maturity alone. Layered validation, not prompt-level care, determines what reaches users. Translation takes minutes; the validation stack is the lasting cost. We derive six testable propositions and ten guidelines, and release the codebook, dataset, and scripts.

RSUP dr. Sitanala is committed to strengthening patient safety culture toward a smart hospital paradigm through an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven innovation named Si Aman EduBot. This interactive chatbot, integrated via WhatsApp and the hospital's proprietary application, was developed to provide real-time education on safety standards, emergency procedures, and digital incident reporting systems for both staff and patients. This study aims to evaluate the impact of Si Aman EduBot implementation on enhancing safety culture within the hospital environment. The evaluation results over a three-month period demonstrated significant achievements, including over 5,000 user interactions, a 35% increase in incident reporting volume, and a 20% improvement in patient safety culture scores from the baseline. The rapid and responsive nature of the chatbot proved effective in increasing staff awareness and fostering an open, blame-free reporting culture. Through its interactive educational features and digital system integration, Si Aman EduBot holds the potential to serve as a national model for building a sustainable patient safety culture. Future developments will focus on integrating voice assistant capabilities and electronic medical records. Keywords: Patient Safety, Educational Chatbot, Digital Incident Reporting, Blame-Free Culture.

documents.abstract: Traditional advertising methods, such as paper posters, banners, and hoardings, require manual design, printing, installation, and maintenance. These activities increase operational effort, material consumption, and the difficulty of updating advertisements. This paper presents SmartAds, a web-based artificial intelligence-powered digital advertisement management platform developed to simplify advertisement creation, pricing, payment-record management, approval, scheduling, and display. The system enables users to generate promotional descriptions and slogans from product details using large language model services. A fallback mechanism involving Groq, an optional local Ollama model, and rule-based generation supports content creation when an AI service is unavailable. Users can select poster or video formats, choose display slots, calculate advertisement costs, and track their submissions. Administrators can approve or reject advertisements before they are scheduled for display. The platform also includes payment-record management, receipt generation, notifications, optional AI avatar-video generation through D-ID, and a browser-based virtual LED display. SmartAds was implemented using Python, Flask, SQLAlchemy, HTML, Bootstrap, and JavaScript. Functional testing documented in the project report covered 45 test cases, all reported as passing. The system demonstrates the feasibility of integrating AI-assisted content generation with digital advertisement workflow management in a controlled proof-of-concept environment.

The scheduling of surgical procedures is a vital and intricate aspect of hospital operations, significantly impacting patient outcomes, financial success, and clinician welfare.Traditional manual scheduling techniques are inadequate for managing the dynamic and unpredictable characteristics of the operating room (OR) environment, resulting in staff fatigue, increased overtime expenses, and a decline in care quality.This study presents a comprehensive artificial intelligence (AI) framework that utilises predictive analytics, multi-objective optimisation, and natural language processing to create dynamic, efficient, and equitable surgical schedules.The technology utilises a continuous feedback loop, assimilating historical and real-time data to optimise operational efficiency while considering human aspects.Conceptual analysis indicates Smart Surgical Scheduling: An AI-Enabled Framework for Operating Room Efficiency and Quality of Care https://iaeme.com/Home/journal/IJCET

Background Due to structural inequities, many migrant workers face adverse health outcomes potentially exposing them to long-term pain issues. However, the extent of current knowledge on chronic pain (>3 months) in this population is unclear. As labor migration policies evolve toward less protective measures, it is essential to gain insights into the experiences and drivers of chronic pain among migrant workers.Aims Drawing on the theoretical framework of intersectionality, this scoping review aimed to synthesize existing knowledge on chronic pain among migrant workers in Canada and the United States. More precisely, we examined evidence related to epidemiology, treatments, lived experiences, and the role of social and structural determinants.Methods This review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews. A search of four databases was followed by a screening and extraction procedure involving four researchers. Relevant findings were reported through quantified and narrative syntheses.Results This scoping review highlights a major gap in understanding pain chronicity among migrant workers. Nine studies met the eligibility criteria. Most studies have focused on occupational health outcomes. Definitions of chronic pain are inconsistent. Only one qualitative study examined migrant workers’ pain trajectories beyond workplace settings. Social and structural determinants were underscored in all studies, including poor working conditions, socioeconomic precarity, unfavorable labor market structure, restrictive immigration policies, racism and discrimination, and gendered inequities.Conclusions This review invites researchers and policymakers to move beyond occupational health approaches to fully appraise and tackle the intersecting structural and political drivers exposing migrant workers to lifelong experiences of chronic pain.

The objective of this study was to determine the influence of social networking use, informal workplace learning, and personal professional development on teachers' attitudes and beliefs towards ICT adoption among public secondary school teachers in Region XI, Philippines. Standardized survey questionnaires were adopted and contextualized to suit the regional educational setting. The instruments were administered to 417 randomly selected teachers using stratified random sampling. This study employed a quantitative, non-experimental research design, using means, Pearson's r, and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) for data analysis. The results revealed generally low to very low levels of social networking usage, informal workplace learning, personal professional development, and attitudes and beliefs toward ICT adoption. Despite these modest levels, significant positive relationships were found between social networking use and teachers' attitudes toward ICT adoption, as well as between personal professional development and these attitudes. Furthermore, the structural equation modeling results indicated that the three independent variables significantly influenced teachers' attitudes and beliefs toward ICT adoption, with social networking usage emerging as the strongest predictor among the constructs. The findings underscore the importance of enhancing digital engagement, strengthening informal learning cultures, and providing sustained professional development initiatives to foster more positive attitudes and stronger readiness for ICT integration in schools.

Observing algorithms, that is, distinguishing algorithms in today's technological and digital society – which is hypercomplex – is indispensable. The emergence of artificial intelligence algorithms has surprised all scientific fields. The education system, for example, is impacted by the possibility of perhaps superficial and certainly very rapid learning of difficult theories that previously took years to master. The science system, on the other hand, besides being impacted by the possibilities, is above all optimistic about the advances. The economic system also sees marked changes. But the legal system is, in a way, apprehensive considering the ethical and normative aspects. The first point relates to decisions. The second point relates specifically to norms and structures of expectations. No one can predict what the consequences will be. But everyone can say that the systems are already revealing great changes and evolutions. Thus, the question arises as to what evolutions have already occurred in the legal system with artificial intelligence.

documents.abstract: TITLE OF THE INVENTION:SOFTWARE-ONLY NEURAL-SYNCHRONIZED ACCESS PROTOCOL (NZAP) FOR MIXED REALITY HEADSETS FEATURING MULTIMODAL SENSOR FUSION, DYNAMIC ERGONOMIC SCALING, AND LOCAL ENCLAVE ZERO-KNOWLEDGE SECURITY APPLICANT / ASSIGNEE (100% OWNER):Meta Platforms, Inc., 1 Hacker Way, Menlo Park, CA 94025, USA — via Assignment of Rights by Dr. Michael Allan Bahtaji — Represented by Facebook Philippines, 11F One World Place, BGC, Taguig INVENTOR FOR ACKNOWLEDGEMENT ONLY:Dr. Michael Allan Bahtaji, Technological University of the Philippines - Manila — No Ownership, No Royalty — Goodwill Defensive Assignment ABSTRACT:A software-orchestrated Neural-Synchronized Access Protocol (NZAP) for head-mounted mixed reality displays (HMDs) that replaces vulnerable external physical controllers and wireless Bluetooth HID peripherals with secure multimodal sensor fusion of optical targeting orientation vectors and wearable electromyography (EMG). The protocol establishes spatial targeting coordinates via optical head-pose orientation vectors or optional eye-tracking arrays, and captures discrete interaction triggers via EMG motor-unit action potentials (MUAPs) synchronized across a 15ms to 50ms temporal coincidence window. Biometric calibration matrices are vectorized and locked inside a hardware Trusted Execution Environment (TEE), purging raw telemetry immediately post-vectorization. Operating within an air-gapped local memory execution boundary, third-party applications receive strictly zero-knowledge abstract input events (e.g., KeyDown, PointerClick). By dynamically throttling high-overhead computer-vision hand-tracking GPU/NPU inference cycles during active temporal coincidence states, system power consumption is significantly reduced without requiring dedicated auxiliary coprocessors. Many pharmacological compounds suffer from poor aqueous solubility, variable bioavailability, fast degradation, unfavorable biodistribution and dose-related side effects, which restrict their therapeutic efficacy. Conventional dosage forms may not achieve the appropriate drug concentrations within the therapeutic window, necessitating the development of improved delivery platforms. Lipid-based nanocarriers, especially solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs) and nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs), provide intriguing methods owing to their biocompatibility, biodegradability and formulation diversity. SLNs are composed of a largely solid lipid matrix supported by surfactants, while NLCs are a mixture of solid and liquid lipids that form a less ordered matrix with more drug accommodation and less drug ejection during storage. This review critically discusses recent advances, with emphasis on literature published during 2021–2026, on the evolution, classification, structural characteristics, formulation components, preparation and characterization, drug-loading and release mechanisms, biological fate, surface engineering, administration routes, and therapeutic applications of SLNs and NLCs. Special attention is paid to safety, regulatory issues, scale-up, commercialization and emerging technologies including artificial intelligence-assisted optimization and microfluidic production. [There has been] considerable preclinical progress but little clinical translation. Long term stability, reproducible large scale manufacturing, regulatory uniformity, and rigorous clinical validation are significant difficulties that need to be systematically investigated.

The integration of artificial intelligence in higher education is occurring at a rapid pace and institutions are still playing catch-up with piecemeal strategies. This chapter presents a governance model that integrates artificial intelligence into curricula, teaching practices, ethical considerations and student learning outcomes. The work is informed by recent research on adaptive learning systems, algorithmic accountability, and outcome-based education (OBE). The model places emphasis on four key elements: curriculum design, faculty training, student data management and institutional governance, outlining roles and decision-making processes. The argument is clear. The incorporation of AI is not a technical issue The framework presented here is grounded in current literature from 2020 to 2024 and incorporates evidence from global pilot programmes in the US, United Kingdom, Australia and India. The chapter concludes that sustainable AI integration depends not on the sophistication of the tools deployed but on the quality of the human decisions made around them.

documents.abstract: Rapid workplace integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping work practices and challenging employees’ self-efficacy and well-being. This mixed-methods study examines these experiences using national survey data ( N = 2109) and qualitative interviews ( N = 54) with Finnish workers. Frequent AI use, AI-induced identity threat, and organizational AI deployment are associated with higher AI strain, whereas AI self-efficacy relates to frequent use, positive AI attitudes, and subjective well-being. Identity threat moderated several of these associations, highlighting the role of professional identity in AI-related experiences. Analysis drawing on Greimas’ semiotic modalities (must, can, know, and want) explains how these patterns are interpreted and negotiated in practice, revealing tensions between perceived self-efficacy and pressures to integrate AI. AI use was often described as voluntary. However, participants anticipated increasing competence demands and responsibility. The findings emphasize the need for organizational strategies that address identity-related challenges and support employee well-being in AI-driven work transformations.

documents.abstract: Introduction Real-time artificial intelligence (AI) decision-support systems are increasingly proposed for use in endoscopic and minimally invasive surgery although how best to present such information intraoperatively is unclear. This study explored surgeon perspectives regarding the user-interface, interpretation and workflow integration of a prototype AI system (CLASSICA-OR) for real-time endoscopic cancer characterization during surgery. Methods Surgeons specialising in minimally invasive gastrointestinal surgery were asked for their first impressions in their evaluation of the CLASSICA-OR system within a high-fidelity surgical simulation environment. For this, participants viewed prerecorded colonoscopic imagery of significant rectal neoplasia while the AI analysis was applied in real-time to the video. Commentary and responses to semi-structured interview were recorded audiovisually for transcription and analysis using qualitative thematic analysis supported by NVivo (Lumivero). Results Eighteen surgeons participated, generating rich qualitative data. Four major themes emerged: (1) AI was viewed as a valuable but evolving decision-support tool; (2) institutional culture, governance and commercial realities were recognised as important determinants of adoption; (3) real-time perfusion-based lesion characterisation (foundational to CLASSICA-OR) was considered promising but with specific challenges; and (4) clarity, usability, transparency and workflow compatibility are surgeon priorities in decision-support displays. Participants emphasised minimised cognitive load, preserved surgeon autonomy, clear communication of uncertainty and seamless workflow integration. Preferences differed between simplified binary outputs and more detailed numerical displays supporting the need for adaptable interfaces. Conclusions Surgeons perceive real-time intraoperative AI decision support as promising but requiring thoughtful user-centred design. They articulate practical development and implementation insights for intraoperative AI systems.

documents.abstract: Technological change is a major development agent across all the layers of contemporary societies, from how economies work to how people access information, how social life is conducted, and even how political institutions work and how decisions are made. In the twenty-first century, digital technologies, ranging from artificial intelligence to mobile connectivity to financial technology and blockchain applications, have revolutionized markets, knowledge, social life, and even the nature of political participation. Sustainability and gender equality, meanwhile, have become twin planks of development frameworks worldwide. The agency of women and girls has been recognized as a transformative force in the development process, and empowerment is understood as central to progress. In turn, gender equality is linked to enhanced economic productivity, poverty reduction, and sustainability. Digital technologies have opened up new paths for women in education, entrepreneurship, employment, and participation. They have helped to reduce some of the traditional structural constraints by expanding women’s access to credit, networks, and information, thereby unleashing the power of women’s agency. But this is far from being the whole story. Women’s access to, skills in using, and power to drive innovation through technology are unequal worldwide. Women’s talent is acutely under-represented in tech-powered jobs, and the digital gender gap constrains women’s empowerment in the digital economy. This chapter explores how sustainability and women’s empowerment through technology relate to each other, with a focus on the Brazilian case, and brings to light some of the key opportunities and challenges.

This is a scoping review protocol that aims to map and characterize the available evidence on the sustainability of complex interventions implemented in long-term care homes. This study adheres to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines and the JBI recommendations for scoping reviews. Searches will be conducted across five electronic databases (MEDLINE, CINAHL, Web of Science, Embase, and LILACS) from inception onward, covering six languages (English, Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian, and German). Primary research studies (quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods) describing sustainable complex interventions in long-term care homes will be eligible. Two reviewers will independently perform study selection and data extraction, utilizing human-supervised artificial intelligence (AI) tools within Covidence to support screening and data audit workflows. Extracted data will be synthesized using descriptive statistics, narrative synthesis, and qualitative content analysis. Identified barriers and facilitators will be inductively extracted and deductively coded into domains of the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. Depending on the volume of data retrieved, findings may be published across multiple papers.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly studied in construction, but its integration with the Circular Economy (CE) remains insufficiently explored. This study maps AI-related construction research and examines its implications for CE within the context of Industry 6.0. A bibliometric analysis of Scopus publications from 2014 to 2024 was conducted using Microsoft Excel and VOSviewer to analyze publication trends, keyword co-occurrence, country contributions, and author productivity. Artificial Intelligence was the dominant keyword, with 291 occurrences, followed by Construction Industry (129), Machine Learning (68), and Sustainable Development (52). China contributed the most publications, while research activity increased substantially after 2020. The findings highlight AI’s potential to support material prediction, waste reduction, material tracking, reuse, and recycling. However, stronger integration of AI research with measurable CE outcomes remains necessary. Future studies should evaluate AI-enabled circular construction using indicators of material efficiency, waste prevention, and resource recovery.

The aging of the global population poses a growing challenge to healthcare systems, as increased longevity is often accompanied by progressive physical and cognitive decline. In the absence of disease-modifying treatments, Active Aging (AA) is promoted as a strategy to preserve autonomy and quality of life through sustained physical, cognitive, and social engagement. While technologies such as extended reality and social robots have already been adopted to support physical training, delivering scalable and engaging cognitive interventions in everyday environments remains an open problem. This paper is grounded in the vision of a holistic Dual-Layer Intervention Framework, in which physical and cognitive training are tightly integrated through embodied interactive systems. Within this broader vision, we present the design and implementation of a Cognitive Intervention Layer based on a large language model–driven conversational agent, deployed on a mixed reality (MR) platform. The proposed solution delivers reminiscence therapy through natural verbal interaction, grounded in the user's physical environment and personal belongings, and is designed to seamlessly interoperate with an existing MR-based Physical Intervention Layer. Preliminary validation through pilot user studies demonstrates the feasibility and usability of the proposed approach, indicating that visually grounded, technology-mediated reminiscence can be effectively integrated into home-based AA routines.

documents.abstract: Systematic reviews are widely regarded as the cornerstone of evidence-based medicine and decision-making, providing structured, transparent, and reproducible syntheses of the available research evidence on a given question. However, traditional systematic review methodologies were developed in an era of comparatively modest scholarly output and now face an evidence base that doubles in size at intervals of less than a decade. The average review requires well over a year of collaborative work, involves screening thousands of records, and relies on manual, cognitively demanding procedures that scale poorly with the volume, velocity, and heterogeneity of contemporary scientific literature. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning, natural language processing, and, more recently, large language models (LLMs), has emerged as a promising response to this challenge of scale. This thesis presents a comprehensive, end-to-end examination of the application of AI throughout the systematic review lifecycle, structured around the four canonical phases of the review workflow: planning; search and study selection; data extraction and critical appraisal; and evidence synthesis and reporting. Drawing on more than two hundred primary sources, including methodological standards established by Cochrane, the PRISMA 2020 statement, five decades of AI research, and empirical studies on the automation of evidence synthesis published between 2006 and 2025, this thesis examines the capabilities and limitations of different classes of AI methods at each stage of the review process. Classical machine learning approaches to relevance screening, supported by two decades of evaluation evidence and shown to reduce screening workload while maintaining high recall, are distinguished from prompt-based LLM approaches. The latter offer broader capabilities, including search query formulation, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment, but their reliability remains insufficient to support unsupervised deployment in rigorous evidence synthesis. The thesis develops a unified analytical framework that maps AI capabilities onto the different phases of systematic reviews; consolidates empirical evidence concerning performance, workload reduction, and failure modes; situates these technologies within Cochrane's methodological standards, the PRISMA 2020 reporting framework, and emerging guidance on the responsible use of generative AI in research; and examines the ethical, epistemological, and organisational implications of delegating knowledge-related tasks to machines. The findings indicate that AI is neither a substitute for the methodological rigour required by systematic reviews nor merely a peripheral convenience. Rather, it constitutes a potentially transformative assistive infrastructure whose safe and effective implementation depends on human-in-the-loop architectures, phase-specific validation, transparent reporting of automation procedures, and the preservation of human judgement as the ultimate authority in evaluating and substantiating knowledge claims. The thesis concludes by presenting structured recommendations for systematic review teams, technology developers, academic journals, and policymakers. It also proposes a research agenda for the emerging field of AI-native evidence synthesis, emphasising the need for rigorous evaluation, methodological transparency, responsible governance, and the continued integration of human expertise into increasingly automated research workflows.

documents.abstract: Drawing on control-value theory and situated expectancy-value theory, this study investigated the relationships between task motivation (i.e., expectancy for success, task values, and task cost), task emotions (i.e., task enjoyment and task anxiety), and cognitive engagement in L2 oral tasks among Chinese post-secondary English learners. A total of 308 Chinese post-secondary students participated in the L2 oral task and completed the task motivation and task emotions questionnaires. Path analysis showed that task value positively predicted learners’ cognitive engagement, and task cost negatively predicted it. While expectancy for success did not predict cognitive engagement directly, its effect was fully mediated by task enjoyment and anxiety. The results also revealed that task anxiety partially mediated the relationships between the other two dimensions of task motivation (task value and task cost) and cognitive engagement. These findings highlight the intricate relationships between motivation, emotions, and cognitive engagement in task-based language teaching, offering both valuable theoretical insights and practical implications for L2 education.

The diffusion of artificial intelligence, data analytics and digital technologies in manufacturing has revived debates about the impact of technological change on work and employment relations. This article examines the implementation of Industry 4.0 technologies in a Spanish train manufacturing company and analyses their implications for workers and their representatives. Drawing on Labour Process Theory and industrial relations literature, the study is based on a qualitative case study including interviews with workers, works council members and technical staff. The findings show that the transition to Industry 4.0 primarily involved the implementation of a Manufacturing Execution System (MES), which digitalised production processes and data collection. Rather than increasing worker autonomy, the system reinforced Taylorist principles through greater standardisation, monitoring and performance measurement. The study also finds that worker representatives played a limited role in regulating technological change despite the existence of formal information and consultation rights. The article argues that technological opacity, institutional constraints and the prioritisation of traditional bargaining issues limit the capacity of worker representatives to influence the governance of workplace technologies.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming higher education, making teacher readiness essential for responsible integration. This paper proposes an empirical framework to examine higher education teachers’ readiness for human-centred AI integration in Assam. Based on UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Teachers, the study focuses on five dimensions: human-centred mindset, AI ethics, AI foundations and applications, AI pedagogy, and AI-supported professional learning, alongside institutional support. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey design is proposed, employing a structured questionnaire and statistical analyses to assess readiness and its influencing factors. Addressing a regional research gap, the study emphasises ethical judgment, pedagogical competence, and human accountability rather than technological adoption alone. As primary data collection is pending, the framework provides a basis for future empirical investigation. The anticipated findings may inform faculty development, institutional AI policies, and responsible AI integration in higher education.

documents.abstract: Digital technology has been used in rehabilitation for decades, from early electronic games and computer-based cognitive training to contemporary virtual and augmented reality, exergaming, robotics, wearables, telerehabilitation, and artificial-intelligence-enabled systems. The field has therefore moved well beyond the question of whether technology can be used in rehabilitation. Existing frameworks address important parts of the problem, including treatment specification, technology classification and selection, therapeutic gaming and virtual-reality decision making, technology-specific clinical utilization, design, adoption, implementation, and co-development. Rather than claiming that these elements are new, this paper asks whether they can be integrated into a technology-agnostic point-of-care reasoning architecture. The Technology-Enhanced Rehabilitation (TER) Framework begins with therapeutic intent: a meaningful goal, an explicit therapeutic target, and a plausible therapeutic strategy. Technology then passes through a therapeutic value checkpoint and may be rejected when a reasonable non-technological alternative is preferable. When technology is justified, clinicians identify the required technological capability, assess fit across person, clinician, technology, and context, and deliberately configure a patient-specific therapeutic experience. TER distinguishes external/technology load, internal response, and a provisional concept of target-relevant therapeutic exposure within an iterative dose-response-adjustment loop. Realized therapeutic value is ultimately judged by meaningful transfer, not technology-native performance. TER is proposed to complement and connect, rather than replace, existing rehabilitation, technology-specific, design, and implementation frameworks.
